title: US Tariffs on India: What the Section 301 Decision Actually Means
seoTitle: US Tariffs on India: Section 301 Explained
excerpt: USTR proposed up to 25 percent tariffs on Indian goods under Section 301, or 17 percent with a trade deal. What the decision says and how India responded.
content:
Quick answer: On 25 November 2026 the United States Trade Representative said 14 economies, including India, had engaged in "unreasonable" manufacturing practices under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. USTR proposed tariffs of up to 25 percent on Indian goods, or 17 percent if India signs a reciprocal trade agreement. India rejected the findings on 25 November, saying there is no structural excess capacity in any sector and that trade disputes should be settled through negotiation. These are proposed tariffs, not yet in force: public comments are due 5 January 2027 and hearings begin 25 January 2027.

What did the United States actually announce?

The US Trade Representative, Jamieson Greer, announced on 25 November 2026 that his office had completed 14 investigations under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The investigations examined what USTR called structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors. USTR determined that the acts, policies and practices of 14 economies are unreasonable and burden or restrict US commerce.

The 14 economies are China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India. USTR had opened 16 investigations on 11 March 2026 but made no determination for Mexico or Norway. For India, the proposed action is a tariff of up to 25 percent on all goods, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain products. USTR also proposed USTR would consider a 17 percent rate if India reaches an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade that is responsive to the findings in this investigation.

The tariffs are proposed, not yet in force; USTR will take public comments and hold hearings in early 2027.

Why did the US use Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974?

Section 301 lets the US government investigate foreign practices it considers unjustifiable, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burden or restrict US commerce. Under Section 302(b), the USTR can start an investigation on its own. After an investigation, the law allows additional duties, import restrictions or suspension of trade concessions.

The legal route matters because of an earlier court ruling. On 20 February 2026 the US Supreme Court decided Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump and Trump v. V.O.S. Selections, holding that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977 does not authorise the president to impose tariffs. That ruling did not prevent tariffs under other statutes such as Section 301. The Congressional Research Service (as of 23 February 2026) recorded that the 6-3 decision invalidated tariffs imposed under that emergency law. The Court's opinion (as of 20 February 2026) said the president was claiming a power to impose tariffs on almost any products, from any countries, in any amounts.

After that ruling, the administration turned to older trade statutes that delegate tariff authority more explicitly to Congress and the USTR. Section 301 is one such route. It does not depend on the emergency powers the Court rejected, but any action under it must still follow the statute's investigation, comment and hearing requirements.

What is "structural excess capacity" and why is India accused of it?

In simple terms, excess capacity means a factory or industry can produce more than domestic demand requires. A factory able to make 150 units when the home market needs 100 may export the remaining 50. USTR's determination (as of 25 November 2026) defines structural excess capacity as persistent excess relative to market-oriented conditions and government intervention, not simply output above demand. It says India's unreasonable acts and policies include industrial plans to expand manufacturing, inadequate labour protections, financial repression policies, sustained market access barriers.

The video explainer by StudyIQ IAS, published 26 November 2026, gives concrete examples of what US officials mean. It points to Make in India, the Production Linked Incentive scheme and Atmanirbhar Bharat as industrial policies the US objects to. It cites financial support for domestic solar panel makers, under which output can rise beyond domestic demand and the extra units are exported at prices US producers say they cannot match. It also describes the US complaint about labour standards: weaker protections can lower costs and make Indian goods cheaper.

The fourth US complaint is persistent barriers to market access, including tariffs, non-tariff barriers and regulations. Agriculture is a long-standing example. The video notes India's position that large numbers of people still depend on farming for their livelihoods, so opening the market fully would put those livelihoods at risk. A seasonal example also matters: manufacturers may make cotton clothing ahead of summer even if demand is low in winter, which can look like excess capacity at a single point in time.

How did India respond?

India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry rejected the allegations on 25 November. According to Business Standard (as of 25 November 2026), India said there is no structural excess capacity in any sector and that trade concerns should be addressed within bilateral trade negotiations. The ministry said India engaged constructively throughout the investigation and that the notice was under examination. The Department of Commerce, which handles these negotiations, has a total allocation of ₹5,873.07 crore in the Union Budget for 2026-27, covering all its work, not these talks alone (India Budget, as of 1 February 2026).

The StudyIQ explainer adds that manufacturing expansion is necessary for a developing economy and that Washington should not dictate how much India produces. This, and the argument that tariffs cannot be imposed by threats, are the video's commentary rather than the official government statement. India has not said it will refuse talks; it has rejected the finding and the method.

What exceptions and rate details matter?

USTR's proposal applies to all goods of India, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain products listed in annexes. The video explainer notes that goods already covered by Section 232 action are exempt, but they are not the only exemptions. The India notice also lists informational materials, donations, accompanied baggage and specified products and raw materials. Section 232 is a separate trade law used for national security concerns.

The proposed 17 percent rate for a country that signs a reciprocal trade agreement is lower than the 25 percent default, but it is still a tariff. The explainer compares it with the proposed 18 percent rate for Malaysia and Bangladesh and says India would do relatively better at 17 percent. That comparison is contextual, not a guarantee: the final rates and product coverage depend on the agreement and on the outcome of the public comment and hearing process.

How does this fit US politics in 2026?

The StudyIQ video frames the tariff push as an attempt by a weakened president to assert authority. It notes that the Republican candidate lost the 2026 mid-term elections and that Democrats won majorities in both chambers in the November midterms, but the new Congress takes office in January 2027. It also notes that President Trump was elected for a second term in 2024 and cannot stand again under the US Constitution, a status often called a lame duck.

These political claims come from the video and should be read as commentary, not as a finding of USTR. The verifiable policy fact is that the Section 301 determinations were issued on 25 November 2026 and that the proposed tariffs are subject to a formal comment and hearing process. The political explanation for why the administration acted is interpretation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are the new US tariffs on India already in force?

No. USTR proposed the action on 25 November 2026. Written comments and requests to appear are due 5 January 2027, and hearings start 25 January 2027.

What is the difference between the 25 percent and 17 percent rates?

The 25 percent rate is the proposed default for Indian goods. The 17 percent rate is what USTR proposes if India signs an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade that addresses the investigation's findings.

Does Section 301 replace the Supreme Court ruling on emergency tariffs?

No. The Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorise presidential tariffs. Section 301 is a different statute that already delegates specific tariff authority to the USTR after an investigation.

What did India say about the excess capacity claim?

India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry said there is no structural excess capacity in any sector and that trade concerns should be settled through bilateral negotiations.

Which countries were investigated but not targeted?

USTR opened 16 investigations on 11 March 2026. It made determinations for 14 economies but made none for Mexico or Norway at this time.
